title: Stoic at home
hookLine: the hive, the household, the people you live with

cards: The sink has a pan in it that's been soaking since Tuesday. Nobody remembers whose it is. It's become a sort of household monument.
Everyone walks past it. Everyone has an opinion about it. Nobody touches it.

If you've lived with roommates, a partner, kids or parents, you know this pan, or its cousin, the empty toilet paper roll. It can be oddly hard to be patient and good in the place where we're most ourselves.
The Stoics thought home was exactly where philosophy gets tested.

teach.h: NOT GOOD FOR THE SWARM, NOR THE BEE.
teach.b: First, the hive. Marcus Aurelius writes, in George Long's 1862 translation: "That which is not good for the swarm, neither is it good for the bee." A bee doesn't thrive by doing well while the hive falls apart.

Whatever helps only me, at the expense of the people I live with, isn't really good for me either. Second, the circles. A later Stoic named Hierocles drew a picture: you at the center of a set of circles.
The first ring is your own mind and body. The next is your closest family, then your wider family, neighbors, your town, and finally all of humanity.

The task, he says, is to draw the circles inward, treating the people in each ring a little more like the ones closer in. The household is the very first ring past your own skin. Third, the word underneath.
Oikeiōsis: making something your own, belonging.
It comes from oikos, the Greek word for household. For the Stoics, care starts with what is closest and grows outward. Home isn't a break from virtue; it's the first ring it has to cross.
Fourth, the pan. A Stoic at home isn't someone who never gets annoyed.

teach.h: ONE THING FOR THE HIVE, NO SCORE.
teach.b: It's someone who asks what's good for the hive, and then does one small thing for it without keeping score.
Wash the pan. Replace the roll. Not as a martyr, not to make a point.
Just as a bee who knows where it lives.

how: Some Stoic practitioners treat the household as the first circle of their care, doing small unasked tasks for the people they live with without keeping score.

o: keeping your house spotless as a moral duty
owning property as the root of a good life
making something your own: care that starts at home

games.q: for the house — tap the pairs.
p: what hurts one hurts the other

s: Marcus wrote that what isn't good for the swarm isn't good for the bee
for the Stoics, home was a break from practicing virtue
it's the first circle, where care begins.
Hierocles told people to push the outer circles further away
he said to draw them inward, treating others more like those closer in.

games.q: the pan has soaked in the sink for days and it isn't yours. what would a Stoic at home do?
o: leave it to make a point
post a sharp note on the fridge
games.why: what's good for the hive is good for the bee; one quiet thing for the house, no martyrdom.

practice: Picture your home and the people in it, or if you live alone, the people closest to you, with you in the middle and them in the first ring. Notice whether any score is being kept, about chores or who gives more, without blame.
Then let one small, unasked-for thing you could do for the house come to mind.

wordCard.voice: Oikeiōsis, the Stoic word for making something your own: the household as the hive and the first circle past your own skin. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, Stoic term: making one's own, belonging; from oikos, household.

carryVoice: Your line: for the house. What's good for the hive is good for the bee. Day six hundred seventy-eight, done.

sources.q: That which is not good for the swarm, neither is it good for the bee.
